planting.note: Broadcast onto a firm, well-prepared seedbed in mid-spring once the danger of frost has passed; light coverage improves germination, and no inoculation is required if lespedeza has grown in the field previously.

directions: Kobe is the standard commercial strain of common lespedeza, selected from stock originally introduced from Kobe, Japan in the early 1900s and still the most widely sold seed source for this species across the Southeast. Broadcast into a firm seedbed in mid-spring, since seedlings emerge slowly and compete poorly with established weeds; once up, the low, branching, trifoliate growth tolerates acidic, droughty, and low-fertility soils where clovers and alfalfa struggle. It is prized on wildlife plantings for its abundant small seed, which quail, dove, and turkey feed on heavily into winter, and its foliage is grazed by deer and cattle through late summer. Mow or graze before hard frost cuts growth short, and allow at least a portion of the stand to set seed if a self-sustaining planting is wanted, since Kobe reseeds readily on suitable ground.

common_name: Serala Sericea Lespedeza (Low-Tannin Perennial Forage and Cover Legume)

planting.note: Broadcast scarified, inoculated seed on a firm spring seedbed; Serala establishes slowly in its seeding year but forms a persistent, deep-rooted stand by the second season.

directions: Serala was one of the first sericea lespedeza releases selected specifically for lower tannin content than unimproved common sericea, giving it noticeably better palatability and digestibility for grazing livestock and wildlife while keeping the species' hallmark drought tolerance and deep taproot. Broadcast inoculated seed into a firm, well-prepared seedbed in spring on poor, acidic, or eroded soils where few other perennial legumes persist, and expect slow first-year establishment followed by a long-lived stand that can be grazed, hayed, or left standing for wildlife cover for a decade or more. Because it reseeds readily and can spread beyond planted areas, confine it to dedicated forage or reclamation plantings and mow before seed set if volunteer spread is a concern. Check state noxious-weed lists before planting, since sericea lespedeza is regulated in some areas.

common_name: AU Grazer Sericea Lespedeza (Rhizomatous Grazing-Tolerant Perennial Legume)

planting.note: Broadcast scarified, inoculated seed into a firm spring seedbed; AU Grazer's spreading rhizomes let it thicken and recover under grazing pressure better than older bunch-type sericea releases.

directions: Developed by Auburn University breeders, AU Grazer was selected for a spreading, rhizomatous growth habit that sets it apart from older bunch-type sericea lespedeza cultivars, allowing stands to thicken over time and better withstand repeated grazing or mowing. It shares the species' deep taproot and exceptional drought tolerance on acidic, low-fertility soils, making it a durable warm-season nitrogen-fixing option for pastures and reclamation sites across the Southeast where few other legumes hold up to heavy use. Broadcast inoculated, scarified seed into a firm seedbed in spring and expect a slow first season while the root system develops before the stand fills in. As with other sericea lespedeza selections, monitor for volunteer spread beyond the planted area and confirm local regulatory status before establishing a stand.

planting.note: Broadcast or hydroseed scarified, inoculated seed onto freshly graded cut-and-fill slopes in spring; Interstate was selected for rapid establishment on the disturbed, low-fertility subsoils typical of highway right-of-way projects.

directions: Interstate takes its name from its long history of use stabilizing highway cut slopes and right-of-way plantings, where its combination of deep, binding roots, drought tolerance, and ability to thrive in raw, infertile subsoil makes it one of the more dependable perennial legumes for erosion control on disturbed ground. Broadcast or hydroseed inoculated seed onto a roughened, freshly graded slope in spring, and expect slow visible growth the first season while the taproot establishes before the planting fills in and begins holding soil in place. Like other sericea lespedeza selections it fixes nitrogen, tolerates acidic and eroded soils poorly suited to other legumes, and persists for many years with minimal maintenance once established, though it is not intended for use in mixed vegetable or rotational cover-crop beds given its persistence and reseeding habit.
sources: state Department of Transportation erosion control seed mix specifications

common_name: AU Lotan Sericea Lespedeza (Improved Low-Tannin Forage and Wildlife Legume)

planting.note: Broadcast scarified, inoculated seed into a firm spring seedbed; AU Lotan was bred at Auburn University for reduced tannin content compared with older sericea releases, improving palatability for grazing livestock and wildlife.

directions: AU Lotan is an Auburn University sericea lespedeza release bred to carry lower tannin levels than earlier cultivars such as common sericea, improving intake and digestibility for cattle, deer, and other wildlife while retaining the species' deep taproot and drought tolerance on acidic, low-fertility ground. Broadcast inoculated, scarified seed into a firm seedbed in spring, expecting a slow establishment year before the stand thickens and becomes productive for grazing, hay, or wildlife cover. It performs best on well-drained, infertile soils where competition from other legumes and grasses is limited, and like other sericea selections it persists for many years and reseeds readily, so plan plantings where a long-term, self-sustaining stand is the goal rather than a short-term rotational cover crop.

planting.note: Broadcast or drill seed into a firm seedbed in early fall in mild-winter regions, or as a fast spring green manure farther north; fenugreek germinates quickly and produces a dense stand of aromatic foliage within weeks.

directions: Long grown as a green manure and forage legume across the Mediterranean, Middle East, and South Asia, fenugreek germinates and canopies quickly, making it a useful short-cycle nitrogen fixer for filling a gap between main-season plantings. Broadcast or drill seed into a firm, well-drained seedbed and keep it evenly moist through the one- to two-week germination window; the trifoliate foliage releases a distinctive maple-like aroma when cut or crushed. In the mild-winter Gulf South it can be sown in early fall as a cool-season cover, growing through winter before being mowed and turned under ahead of spring planting; farther north it performs best as a quick spring or summer green manure terminated before hard freeze or seed set. Incorporate the tender top growth while still succulent for the fastest nitrogen release and breakdown.

planting.note: Broadcast or drill into a firm, moist seedbed after all danger of frost; Silverhull's shorter, more shatter-resistant seed heads let it stand a bit longer than Japanese-type buckwheat before dropping seed.

directions: Silverhull is an older, small-seeded buckwheat strain long favored in the Southeast and Appalachia for its quicker maturity and sturdier, less shatter-prone seed head compared with taller Japanese-type buckwheat. Broadcast or drill seed into a firm, moist seedbed once the soil has warmed after frost, and expect rapid emergence and a full canopy within a few weeks that smothers summer weeds and scavenges phosphorus from the soil. Its abundant small white flowers draw honeybees and other pollinators over a long summer bloom period, making it a popular dual-purpose planting for beekeepers and gardeners alike. Mow or turn it under at first bloom for the best soil-building value, or allow a short second flush by cutting before hard seed set if a fall planting window remains.

common_name: Hykon Rose Clover (Standard Improved Reseeding Rose Clover)

planting.note: Broadcast seed in fall at 8-12 lbs per acre into a firm seedbed; Hykon is the standard commercial rose clover cultivar, selected for improved seedling vigor and stand uniformity over common unimproved rose clover seed. Inoculate with Rhizobium leguminosarum biovar. trifolii before sowing.

directions: Hykon is the widely planted named selection of rose clover used throughout California, Texas, and the Gulf South wherever a hardy, self-reseeding winter annual legume is needed on dry, acidic, or low-fertility rangeland soils. Broadcast inoculated seed onto a firm seedbed in fall so plants can establish before winter, then rely on the clover's hard seed coat and reseeding habit to carry the stand through the summer dry season without replanting. Like the straight species, it fixes nitrogen through root nodules, tolerates grazing and drought once established, and produces fuzzy rose-pink flower heads that draw pollinators in spring. Mow or graze at early bloom for the greatest soil-building benefit, leaving enough seed heads to mature for next year's stand.

common_name: Salina Strawberry Clover (Saline- and Wet-Soil-Tolerant Perennial Clover)

planting.note: Direct sow into moist to wet, heavy or saline-affected soil in spring; inoculate seed with clover-type Rhizobium before sowing. Salina was selected for improved performance on wet, saline, and alkaline soils that limit most other clovers.

directions: Salina is a named selection of strawberry clover developed for reliable establishment on wet, saline, and alkaline soils where other clovers and cover-crop legumes typically fail, making it a useful option for irrigated pasture edges, drainage-affected fields, and reclaimed saline seep areas. Direct sow inoculated seed into moist, heavy soil in spring and expect a low, creeping perennial mat that spreads by stolons rather than an upright stand, tolerating both standing water and periods of salt stress better than white or red clover. Once established it fixes nitrogen, persists for years under mowing or light grazing, and produces the species' distinctive inflated, strawberry-like seed heads that give it its common name. It is best suited to permanent plantings such as living mulches, waterway buffers, or problem wet spots rather than annual rotation beds.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service Plant Materials Program
